Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease commonly associated with Xanthomonas species. It can cause small, water-soaked leaf spots that become brown or dark and may lead to leaf drop.
management: Remove heavily affected plant material where practical.
Avoid handling plants when foliage is wet.
Avoid overhead irrigation when possible.
Improve airflow around plants.
Consult local agricultural guidance for approved control options.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or transplants.
Clean tools and equipment between plantings.
Rotate with non-host crops where practical.
Monitor plants regularly for early symptoms.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.precautions: Bacterial diseases may not respond to fungicides intended for fungal pathogens. Confirm the diagnosis before selecting a treatment.

management: Continue regular plant monitoring.
Maintain appropriate irrigation.
Provide balanced nutrition based on crop needs.

Pepper__bell___healthy.precautions: A healthy prediction does not guarantee that the entire plant is free of disease or pests.

Potato___Early_blight.description: A fungal disease commonly caused by Alternaria solani. It often produces brown lesions with concentric rings, especially on older leaves.
management: Remove severely affected foliage where appropriate.
Reduce prolonged leaf wetness.
Maintain adequate plant nutrition.
Improve airflow where practical.
Seek local advice about approved fungicide programs if needed.
prevention: Monitor older leaves for early symptoms.
Potato___Early_blight.precautions: Early blight can resemble other leaf-spot diseases. Confirm symptoms before treatment.

Potato___Late_blight.description: A serious disease caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans. It can produce rapidly expanding dark lesions and may also affect tubers.
management: Inspect nearby plants promptly for similar symptoms.
Avoid moving infected plant material between fields.
Reduce prolonged foliage wetness where possible.
Follow local extension guidance for urgent disease management.
Use only locally approved crop-protection products when advised.
prevention: Eliminate volunteer potatoes and infected cull piles.
Monitor weather conditions favorable to late blight.
Inspect crops frequently during cool, wet periods.
Follow locally recommended preventive management programs.
Potato___Late_blight.precautions: Late blight can spread rapidly and cause major crop losses. Seek prompt professional advice when suspected.

Potato___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with healthy potato foliage within the model's supported categories.
management: Maintain regular crop monitoring.
Provide appropriate irrigation and nutrition.
Inspect plants for pests and disease symptoms.
Maintain good field hygiene.
Potato___healthy.precautions: A healthy leaf prediction does not rule out diseases affecting other plant parts or tubers.

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease associated with Xanthomonas species. It may produce small dark leaf spots and can affect stems and fruits.
management: Avoid working with plants while foliage is wet.
Remove severely affected plant material where appropriate.
Reduce overhead irrigation.
Improve airflow around plants.
Consult local agricultural guidance for approved management options.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.precautions: Confirm bacterial spot before treatment. Management differs from that of fungal leaf diseases.

Tomato_Early_blight.description: A fungal disease commonly associated with Alternaria species. It often causes brown leaf spots with concentric rings and surrounding yellowing.
management: Remove heavily affected lower leaves when practical.
Avoid splashing water onto foliage.
Use mulch to reduce soil splash.
Improve airflow around plants.
Consult local guidance about approved fungicides if needed.
prevention: Remove or manage infected crop debris.
Tomato_Early_blight.precautions: Several tomato diseases produce similar leaf spots. Confirm the diagnosis before applying treatments.

Tomato_Late_blight.description: A serious disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. It can produce rapidly expanding, water-soaked or dark lesions on leaves and stems, and may damage fruit.
management: Inspect surrounding tomato and potato plants immediately.
Avoid moving potentially infected plant material.
Reduce prolonged foliage wetness where possible.
Seek prompt local agricultural advice.
Follow locally approved disease-management recommendations.
prevention: Monitor crops during cool, humid weather.
Remove volunteer host plants and manage infected debris safely.
Tomato_Late_blight.precautions: Suspected late blight requires prompt attention because it can spread rapidly. Confirm the diagnosis with a qualified agricultural professional.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva. It commonly produces yellow patches on upper leaf surfaces and olive-green to brown mold on the undersides, especially in humid conditions.
management: Improve greenhouse or growing-area ventilation.
Reduce excessive humidity.
Avoid wetting leaves unnecessarily.
Remove heavily affected foliage where practical.
Consult local guidance if additional control is needed.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.precautions: Leaf mold is favored by humid conditions. Environmental management is an important part of control.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici. It commonly causes numerous small leaf spots with pale centers and darker margins.
management: Remove heavily affected lower leaves where practical.
Avoid splashing water onto foliage.
Apply mulch to reduce soil splash.
Improve airflow around plants.
Seek local guidance about approved control measures.
prevention: Monitor lower leaves for early symptoms.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.precautions: Septoria leaf spot can resemble other tomato leaf-spot diseases. Confirm symptoms before treatment.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.description: An infestation by the two-spotted spider mite, Tetranychus urticae. Feeding may cause tiny pale spots, yellowing, bronzing, and fine webbing.
management: Inspect leaf undersides for mites and webbing.
Remove heavily infested leaves where practical.
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide use.
Support beneficial natural enemies when appropriate.
Consult local integrated pest management guidance.
prevention: Monitor crops regularly, especially during hot, dry weather.
Inspect new plants before introducing them.
Manage nearby weeds and alternative hosts.
Encourage beneficial predatory mites where appropriate.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.precautions: Spider mites are pests, not fungal pathogens. Fungicides intended for fungal diseases are not an appropriate mite treatment.

Tomato__Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease commonly caused by Corynespora cassiicola. It may cause brown leaf lesions with concentric rings.
management: Remove heavily affected foliage where appropriate.
Improve airflow between plants.
Reduce prolonged leaf wetness.
Manage infected crop residue.
Consult local guidance about approved control options.
prevention: Monitor leaves regularly for developing spots.
Tomato__Target_Spot.precautions: Target spot can resemble early blight and other leaf diseases. Confirm the diagnosis before treatment.

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.description: A viral disease commonly transmitted by whiteflies. Affected plants may show yellowing, upward leaf curling, stunted growth, and reduced fruit production.
management: Inspect plants for whiteflies.
Remove severely infected plants when locally recommended.
Manage whitefly populations using integrated pest management.
Control weeds that may serve as virus hosts.
Seek local advice about resistant varieties and vector control.
prevention: Choose resistant or tolerant varieties when available.
Use suitable insect-exclusion measures where practical.
Remove volunteer tomato plants and relevant weeds.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.precautions: There is no treatment that cures an already virus-infected plant. Management focuses on limiting spread and protecting healthy plants.

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A viral disease that may cause mottled light- and dark-green patterns, leaf distortion, and reduced plant vigor.
management: Avoid handling healthy plants after touching suspected infected plants.
Clean hands, tools, and equipment appropriately.
Remove infected plants when recommended by local guidance.
Avoid using infected plants for propagation.
Seek confirmation from an agricultural diagnostic service.
prevention: Use certified healthy seeds and transplants.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.precautions: There is no cure for systemic tomato mosaic virus infection. Sanitation and prevention are essential.
